answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS cascode common-source amplifier:

- \(M_1\): common-source input transistor  
- \(M_2\): common-gate cascode transistor  
- \(I_1\): active current-source load  
- \(X\): drain of \(M_1\) and source of \(M_2\)

Assume \(V_{b1}\) is a stiff DC bias and is AC-grounded for small-signal analysis.

## DC bias

If both MOSFETs are in saturation and there is no external output load,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1 .
\]

Using

\[
I_D=\frac{1}{2}\beta V_{OV}^2,
\]

the required overdrives are

\[
V_{OV1}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_1}},\qquad
V_{OV2}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_2}}.
\]

Thus the input DC bias should be approximately

\[
V_{in,Q}=V_{T1}+V_{OV1}.
\]

Since

\[
V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_X,
\]

the cascode bias sets node \(X\):

\[
V_X \simeq V_{b1}-V_{T2}-V_{OV2}.
\]

If body effect exists in \(M_2\), use \(V_{T2}(V_X)\) instead of a constant threshold voltage.

For both devices to remain saturated,

\[
V_X\geq V_{OV1}
\]

and

\[
V_{out}-V_X\geq V_{OV2}.
\]

Hence the output low-voltage limit is approximately

\[
V_{out,\min}\simeq V_X+V_{OV2}.
\]

Usually \(V_{b1}\) is selected so that \(V_X\approx V_{OV1}\), giving

\[
V_{b1}\approx V_{T2}+V_{OV1}+V_{OV2},
\]

and therefore

\[
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

At the upper end, the current source must remain in compliance:

\[
V_{out,\max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{\text{comp},I_1}.
\]

A purely ideal current source and ideal square-law MOS model do not uniquely determine the DC value of \(V_{out}\); any value within the saturation/compliance range is possible. In a real circuit, finite \(r_o\), load circuitry, or common-mode feedback establishes the quiescent output voltage.

---

## Small-signal analysis

Let

\[
g_{oi}=\frac{1}{r_{oi}},
\]

and include body effect of \(M_2\), if relevant, through

\[
g_c=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}.
\]

Set \(g_{mb2}=0\) if body effect is neglected.

Let \(g_L\) be the total small-signal conductance connected from the output to AC ground. For the shown circuit,

\[
g_L=\frac{1}{r_{o,I_1}},
\]

where \(r_{o,I_1}\) is the output resistance of the current source. For an ideal current source, \(g_L=0\).

The small-signal nodal equations are

\[
(g_{o1}+g_c+g_{o2})v_x-g_{o2}v_o=-g_{m1}v_i
\]

and

\[
-(g_c+g_{o2})v_x+(g_{o2}+g_L)v_o=0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{v_i}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}(g_c+g_{o2})}
{g_{o1}g_{o2}+g_L(g_{o1}+g_c+g_{o2})}
}
\]

The minus sign shows that the stage is inverting: an increase in \(V_{in}\) increases the pull-down current and reduces \(V_{out}\).

For an ideal current source load, \(g_L=0\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]
}
\]

and, for \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx
-g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}
}
\]

---

## Output resistance

Looking into the drain of \(M_2\), the resistance of the cascode stack is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{cas}}
=
r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}
}
\]

Thus the total output resistance is approximately

\[
\boxed{
R_{out}=R_{\text{cas}}\parallel r_{o,I_1}
}
\]

If \(g_m r_o\gg 1\),

\[
R_{\text{cas}}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]

The usual approximate voltage gain is then

\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx -g_{m1}
\left[
(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}
\parallel r_{o,I_1}
\right]
}
\]

---

## Main role of \(M_2\)

\(M_2\) keeps node \(X\) relatively constant and reduces variations in \(V_{DS1}\). This suppresses channel-length modulation in \(M_1\), greatly increases output resistance, and hence provides much larger gain than a single common-source transistor.

The input resistance is ideally very high:

\[
R_{in}\approx \infty,
\]

apart from MOS gate capacitances and any external bias network.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source NMOS and M2 as the common-gate NMOS cascode, and derives the equivalent ideal-load gain expression.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an **NMOS cascode common-source stage**:

- \(M_1\): common-source input transistor  
- \(M_2\): common-gate cascode transistor  
- \(I_1\): pull-up bias-current source  
- \(V_{b1}\): cascode bias voltage  
- \(X\): internal cascode node  

A positive change in \(v_{in}\) increases the current in \(M_1\), so \(v_{out}\) falls. Thus the stage is inverting.

## DC bias conditions

Assume both MOSFETs operate in saturation and define

\[
V_{OV1}=V_{GS1}-V_{T1},\qquad
V_{OV2}=V_{GS2}-V_{T2}.
\]

For a branch current \(I_1\),

\[
I_1 \simeq \frac{\beta_1}{2}V_{OV1}^2
\simeq \frac{\beta_2}{2}V_{OV2}^2 .
\]

Hence,

\[
V_{in,Q}=V_{T1}+V_{OV1}
\]

and the cascode bias sets node \(X\) approximately to

\[
V_X=V_{b1}-V_{T2}-V_{OV2}.
\]

To keep \(M_1\) in saturation,

\[
V_X\geq V_{OV1},
\]

so a minimum useful cascode bias is approximately

\[
V_{b1}\geq V_{T2}+V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

The output-voltage compliance range is

\[
V_{out}\geq V_X+V_{OV2}.
\]

If \(V_X\) is chosen near \(V_{OV1}\), then

\[
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

The upper limit is set by the compliance of \(I_1\). If \(I_1\) is implemented by a PMOS current source,

\[
V_{out,\max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{OV,I}.
\]

Thus, compared with a simple common-source stage, the cascode costs roughly one additional overdrive voltage of output swing.

---

## Small-signal analysis

Assume \(V_{b1}\) is an AC ground. Define

\[
g_{o1}=\frac{1}{r_{o1}},\qquad
g_{o2}=\frac{1}{r_{o2}},\qquad
g_{oI}=\frac{1}{r_{oI}},
\]

where \(r_{oI}\) is the output resistance of the current source. For an ideal \(I_1\), \(g_{oI}=0\).

Let

\[
g_c=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}
\]

with \(g_{mb2}=0\) if body effect is neglected. The low-frequency nodal equations are

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
g_{o1}+g_c+g_{o2} & -g_{o2}\\
-(g_c+g_{o2}) & g_{o2}+g_{oI}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
v_x\\v_{out}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-g_{m1}v_{in}\\0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}(g_c+g_{o2})}
{g_{o1}(g_{o2}+g_{oI})+(g_c+g_{o2})g_{oI}}
}
\]

The negative sign confirms inversion.

### Output resistance

With \(v_{in}=0\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{out}
=
r_{oI}\parallel
\left[
r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_c r_{o1}r_{o2}
\right]
}
\]

Ignoring body effect,

\[
R_{out}
=
r_{oI}\parallel
\left[
r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}
\right].
\]

For \(g_{m2}r_{o1}\gg 1\) and \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg 1\),

\[
R_{out}\approx r_{oI}\parallel
\left(g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\right).
\]

Thus the cascode increases the output resistance by approximately a factor of \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\).

### Usual gain approximation

Since the effective transconductance is approximately \(g_{m1}\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v \approx
-g_{m1}
\left[
r_{oI}\parallel
\left(g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\right)
\right]
}
\]

For an ideal current source load, \(r_{oI}\to\infty\),

\[
A_v \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]

The exact result for an ideal \(I_1\) is

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left(1+g_c r_{o2}\right).
\]

---

## Main purpose of \(M_2\)

\(M_2\) keeps node \(X\) relatively insensitive to changes in \(v_{out}\). Hence, \(V_{DS1}\) changes very little, reducing the channel-length-modulation effect in \(M_1\). This gives:

- much larger output resistance,
- much larger voltage gain,
- reduced Miller effect at the drain of \(M_1\),

at the expense of output-voltage headroom.

If all \(r_o\)'s are treated as infinite and \(I_1\) is ideal, the circuit has no finite small-signal output conductance; \(v_{out}\) is then not uniquely established by the ideal square-law model and will eventually move to a compliance or saturation limit in a real circuit.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source NMOS and M2 as the common-gate NMOS cascode, and gives the correct gain, including the ideal-load expression. The output-resistance and inversion explanations are consistent with the cascode topology.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS **cascode common-source stage**:

- \(M_1\) is the input common-source transistor.
- \(M_2\) is a common-gate cascode device biased by \(V_{b1}\).
- \(I_1\) supplies the dc bias current.
- \(X\) is the internal cascode node.
- The stage is inverting: an increase in \(V_{\text{in}}\) tends to pull \(V_{\text{out}}\) downward.

Assume initially that both MOSFETs are in saturation, body effect is neglected, and \(V_{b1}\) is an ac ground.

---

## 1. DC bias and headroom

At the intended bias point,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1
\]

and, neglecting channel-length modulation,

\[
V_{OV1}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_1}},
\qquad
V_{OV2}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_2}} .
\]

Thus,

\[
V_{\text{in,Q}}=V_{T1}+V_{OV1}
\]

and the cascode bias sets node \(X\):

\[
V_X=V_{b1}-V_{T2}-V_{OV2}.
\]

For \(M_1\) to remain saturated,

\[
V_X \geq V_{OV1}.
\]

Therefore, \(V_{b1}\) should satisfy approximately

\[
V_{b1}\geq V_{T2}+V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

For \(M_2\) to remain saturated,

\[
V_{\text{out}}-V_X \geq V_{OV2},
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}\gtrsim V_{b1}-V_{T2}}.
\]

If \(V_{b1}\) is chosen at its minimum useful value, the lowest output voltage is roughly

\[
V_{\text{out,min}}\simeq V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

The upper output swing is limited by the compliance voltage of the current source:

\[
V_{\text{out,max}}\lesssim V_{DD}-V_{\text{comp},I_1}.
\]

---

## 2. Small-signal output resistance

Let

\[
g_{oi}=\frac{1}{r_{oi}},
\]

and define

\[
D=g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}.
\]

With \(v_{\text{in}}=0\), the resistance looking into the drain of \(M_2\) is

\[
R_{\text{cas}}
=
\frac{D}{g_{o1}g_{o2}}
=
r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{cas}}
=
r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}
}
\]

and, for \(g_{m2}r_o\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{cas}}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
}
\]

This is the main benefit of the cascode: \(M_2\) keeps \(V_X\) relatively insensitive to output-voltage changes, thereby reducing the variation of \(M_1\)'s drain current.

Indeed, with \(v_{\text{in}}=0\),

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{\text{out}}}
=
\frac{g_{o2}}{g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
\approx
\frac{1}{g_{m2}r_{o2}}.
\]

Hence \(v_x\) moves much less than \(v_{\text{out}}\).

If the current source \(I_1\) has finite output resistance \(r_I\), then

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}=R_{\text{cas}}\parallel r_I.
}
\]

For an ideal current source, \(r_I\rightarrow \infty\), so \(R_{\text{out}}=R_{\text{cas}}\).

---

## 3. Voltage gain

The effective transconductance from \(v_{\text{in}}\) to output current is

\[
G_{m,\text{eff}}
=
g_{m1}
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{o2}}
{g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
A_v\equiv\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}
=
-G_{m,\text{eff}}
\left(R_{\text{cas}}\parallel r_I\right).
\]

The exact low-frequency result is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
-\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{o2})}
{g_{o1}g_{o2}+
g_I(g_{m2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2})}
}
\]

where \(g_I=1/r_I\).

For an ideal current source load, \(g_I=0\),

\[
A_v
=
-\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{o2})}{g_{o1}g_{o2}}
=
-g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2}).
\]

If \(g_mr_o\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
}
\]

More commonly, with a nonideal current-source load,

\[
\boxed{
A_v \approx
-g_{m1}
\left[
r_I\parallel
\left(g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\right)
\right].
}
\]

---

## 4. Important ideal-model caveat

If channel-length modulation is ignored entirely,

\[
r_{o1},r_{o2}\rightarrow\infty,
\]

and \(I_1\) is also an ideal current source, then the circuit has no finite small-signal output conductance. In that idealized model,

\[
R_{\text{out}}\rightarrow\infty,
\qquad
|A_v|\rightarrow\infty.
\]

Physically, this means that the output voltage is not determined by dc current equations alone; a finite \(r_o\), a real current-source resistance, an external load, or capacitances must be included. answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect depends on the voltage gain **across the parasitic feedback capacitance**, not simply on the overall gain of the amplifier.

In a common-source/common-emitter stage, the gate-drain or base-collector capacitance (\(C_{gd}\) or \(C_\mu\)) connects the input to the high-gain output:

\[
C_{\text{in, Miller}} = C_{gd}(1-A_v)
\]

Since \(A_v\) is large and negative, this becomes roughly

\[
C_{gd}(1+|A_v|),
\]

so a small parasitic capacitance appears much larger at the input.

In a cascode, the lower transistor’s drain/collector is connected to the source/emitter of an upper common-gate/common-base transistor. That upper transistor presents a low small-signal impedance at this internal node, approximately

\[
Z_x \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

Therefore, the lower transistor’s drain/collector voltage has little gain relative to its input. For a MOS cascode, approximately,

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}},
\]

which is often of order \(-1\), rather than \(-10\), \(-100\), etc. Thus the lower device’s \(C_{gd}\) is multiplied only modestly:

\[
C_{\text{in due to }C_{gd1}}
\approx
C_{gd1}\left(1+\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right).
\]

For matched devices, this is about \(2C_{gd1}\), not \(C_{gd1}(1+|A_v|)\) with a large voltage gain.

The large output voltage swing occurs at the drain/collector of the **upper** cascode device. Its gate/base is normally at AC ground, so its gate-drain or base-collector capacitance mainly appears as an output capacitance rather than feeding the output signal back to the input.

So, a cascode reduces Miller effect because it isolates the input transistor’s drain/collector from the large output-voltage swing. The Miller effect is not eliminated, but the capacitance is no longer multiplied by the full amplifier gain.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode internal node and the resulting modest gain across the lower device’s Cgd (about −gm1/gm2, roughly −1), so its Miller multiplication is about 2 rather than the full stage gain. The minor omission of body effect does not change the explanation.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is large when a capacitance bridges an input node and a **high-gain, inverted output node**.

For a capacitance such as MOS \(C_{gd}\) or BJT \(C_{\mu}=C_{bc}\),

\[
C_{\text{seen at input}} \approx C(1-A_v)
\]

where \(A_v\) is the voltage gain from the input to the other terminal of that capacitor. In a common-source/common-emitter stage, that gain is large and negative, so

\[
C_{\text{in}} \approx C_{gd}(1+|A_v|),
\]

which can be much larger than the physical capacitance.

In a cascode, the lower transistor’s drain/collector is connected to the source/emitter of an upper common-gate/common-base transistor. The upper device presents a relatively low small-signal impedance at that node, roughly

\[
R_x \sim \frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

Therefore, the lower transistor’s drain/collector voltage has only a small-to-moderate gain relative to the input—not the large overall voltage gain of the amplifier. Approximately,

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{\text{in}}} \sim -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}},
\]

rather than \(-g_{m1}R_{\text{out}}\). Thus the lower device’s \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_{\mu}\) is multiplied by only an order-unity factor, not by the full amplifier gain.

The large output voltage swing occurs at the drain/collector of the **upper** device. Since that node is separated from the input by the common-gate/common-base transistor, it does not feed back strongly through the lower transistor’s gate-drain/base-collector capacitance.

So, a cascode does not eliminate parasitic capacitances, but it prevents the high output voltage gain from appearing across the input device’s feedback capacitance. This greatly reduces Miller multiplication and improves high-frequency bandwidth.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and the resulting order-unity gain across the lower transistor’s feedback capacitance, rather than the full amplifier gain. It also makes clear that Miller multiplication is reduced, not eliminated.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect depends on the voltage gain **across the particular parasitic capacitance**, not simply on the amplifier’s overall gain.

For a capacitance \(C_f\) between an input node \(v_i\) and another node \(v_x=A_xv_i\),

\[
C_{\text{seen at input}} = C_f(1-A_x).
\]

In a common-source/common-emitter stage, the gate-drain or base-collector capacitance (\(C_{gd}\) or \(C_\mu\)) connects the input to the output. Since the output is inverted and has large gain,

\[
A_x \approx -|A_v|,
\]

so the apparent input capacitance becomes roughly

\[
C_f(1+|A_v|),
\]

which can be much larger than the physical capacitance.

In a cascode:

- The lower transistor’s \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_\mu\) connects its input to the **internal drain/collector node**, not directly to the final output.
- The upper common-gate/common-base transistor presents a low impedance at that internal node—roughly on the order of \(1/g_{m2}\).
- Therefore, the large output-voltage swing occurs at the drain/collector of the upper transistor, while the lower transistor’s drain/collector has only a small or modest voltage gain relative to its input.

Thus the lower device’s capacitance sees

\[
A_x = \frac{v_{\text{internal}}}{v_i}
\]

rather than the large overall output gain. In a simple model, \(A_x\) may be about \(-g_{m1}/g_{m2}\), rather than \(-g_mR_{\text{out}}\). Its Miller multiplication is therefore small—often only a factor near 1–2 instead of tens or hundreds.

Also, the upper transistor’s \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_\mu\) is connected to a gate/base that is usually AC-grounded, so it mainly appears as an output capacitance rather than an input-to-output feedback capacitance.

So, a cascode preserves high voltage gain while preventing that high-gain output swing from being fed back through the lower transistor’s gate-drain/base-collector capacitance.

It gives the resulting Miller factor near 1–2, rather than treating the effect as eliminated, while distinguishing this from the cascode’s high overall gain.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assuming the usual interpretation of the symbols, \(M_1\) is a pMOS device and \(M_2\) is an nMOS device:

| Device | Source | Gate | Drain |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(M_1\) | \(V_{DD}\) | \(V_{b2}\) | \(V_{\text{out}}\) |
| \(M_2\) | \(V_{\text{in}}\) | \(V_{b1}\) | \(V_{\text{out}}\) |

Thus, \(M_2\) is operated as a **common-gate amplifier**, and \(M_1\) is a biased pMOS active load/current source. Notice that \(V_{\text{in}}\) is applied to the source of \(M_2\), not to its gate.

## DC bias conditions

Define the overdrives

\[
V_{OV1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|
\]

\[
V_{OV2}=V_{b1}-V_{\text{in}}-V_{TN}
\]

For both devices to conduct in saturation,

\[
V_{OV1}>0,\qquad V_{OV2}>0
\]

and, neglecting channel-length modulation,

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{\beta_p}{2}V_{OV1}^{2}
\]

\[
I_{D2}=\frac{\beta_n}{2}V_{OV2}^{2}
\]

At the quiescent point, with no external dc load,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\beta_p\left(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|\right)^2
=
\beta_n\left(V_{b1}-V_{\text{in}}-V_{TN}\right)^2.
\]

Equivalently, the input dc level required for current balance is

\[
V_{\text{in},Q}
=
V_{b1}-V_{TN}
-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_p}{\beta_n}}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|\right).
\]

The saturation requirements impose the output-voltage range

\[
V_{\text{out}} \ge V_{\text{in}}+V_{OV2}
=V_{b1}-V_{TN}
\]

and

\[
V_{\text{out}} \le V_{DD}-V_{OV1}
=V_{b2}+|V_{TP}|.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
V_{b1}-V_{TN}
\le V_{\text{out}}
\le
V_{b2}+|V_{TP}|
}
\]

is the region in which both MOSFETs remain saturated.

With an ideal square-law model and \(\lambda=0\), the exact dc value of \(V_{\text{out}}\) is not determined once the two saturation currents are equal. In reality, channel-length modulation, a load, or one transistor entering triode determines the dc output voltage.

---

## Small-signal analysis

For small signals, take \(V_{DD}\), \(V_{b1}\), and \(V_{b2}\) as ac ground. Let

\[
g_{o1}=\frac{1}{r_{o1}}, \qquad g_{o2}=\frac{1}{r_{o2}}.
\]

If an output load \(R_L\) is present, the small-signal output equation is

\[
\left(g_{o1}+g_{o2}+\frac{1}{R_L}\right)v_{\text{out}}
=
\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}\right)v_{\text{in}}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}
{g_{o1}+g_{o2}+1/R_L}
}
\]

and, for \(g_m\gg g_o\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v \simeq
+\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)
\left(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L\right)
}
\]

The gain is positive: an increase in \(V_{\text{in}}\) raises the source voltage of \(M_2\), reduces \(V_{GS2}\), reduces the current pulled by \(M_2\), and therefore allows \(V_{\text{out}}\) to rise.

The usual approximate resistances are

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}}
\]

and, with the input ac-grounded,

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}\simeq r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}}.
\]

So the circuit is a non-inverting common-gate voltage amplifier with low input resistance and high output resistance. Numerical values require the transistor parameters, dc input level, bias voltages, channel-length modulation, and any output load.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-driven common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, the bias voltages, positive gain, and low input resistance; its gain expression is equivalent to the required gm2(ro1||ro2) approximation. The input-resistance simplification is nonessential under the full-credit rule.

answer.text:
\(M_1\) is a pMOS active-load device and \(M_2\) is an nMOS device. The important observation is that \(V_{\text{in}}\) is applied to the **source** of \(M_2\), while \(V_{b1}\) is its gate bias. Thus, this is a **common-gate amplifier** with a pMOS current-source load, not a common-source inverter.

Assume both transistors operate in saturation, \(V_{DD}\), \(V_{b1}\), and \(V_{b2}\) are ideal bias voltages, and define

\[
V_{OV2}=V_{b1}-V_{\text{in},Q}-V_{TN}
\]

\[
V_{OV1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|
\]

where \(V_{\text{in},Q}\) is the dc input/source voltage of \(M_2\).

## DC bias

Ignoring channel-length modulation,

\[
I_D=
\frac{\beta_n}{2}
\left(V_{b1}-V_{\text{in},Q}-V_{TN}\right)^2
\]

for \(M_2\), and

\[
I_D=
\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|\right)^2
\]

for \(M_1\).

Therefore, for equal dc currents,

\[
V_{\text{in},Q}
=
V_{b1}-V_{TN}
-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_p}{\beta_n}}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|\right).
\]

Equivalently, the bias voltages can be chosen as

\[
V_{b1}=V_{\text{in},Q}+V_{TN}+V_{OV2}
\]

\[
V_{b2}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|-V_{OV1}.
\]

For both devices to remain saturated,

\[
V_{O,Q}-V_{\text{in},Q}\geq V_{OV2}
\]

and

\[
V_{DD}-V_{O,Q}\geq V_{OV1}.
\]

Hence the allowable output range is approximately

\[
\boxed{
V_{b1}-V_{TN}
\;\leq\;
V_O
\;\leq\;
V_{b2}+|V_{TP}|
}
\]

assuming no body effect. If the nMOS bulk is tied to \(V_{SS}\), use the source-dependent threshold voltage \(V_{TN}(V_{SB})\).

With ideal square-law devices and \(\lambda=0\), the output dc voltage is not uniquely determined if both devices are saturated: both behave as ideal current sources. In practice, channel-length modulation, an output load, or feedback fixes \(V_{O,Q}\).

---

## Small-signal voltage gain

For small-signal analysis, \(V_{DD}\), \(V_{b1}\), and \(V_{b2}\) are ac ground.

Define

\[
G_m=g_{m2}+g_{mb2},
\]

where \(g_{mb2}=0\) if the bulk of \(M_2\) is tied to its source.

The pMOS \(M_1\) contributes mainly its output resistance \(r_{o1}\); its \(g_m\) does not appear because its gate and source are both at ac ground.

With an output load \(R_L\),

\[
\left(\frac{1}{r_{o1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}+\frac{1}{R_L}\right)v_o
=
\left(G_m+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}\right)v_{in}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_{in}}
=
\frac{G_m+1/r_{o2}}
{1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}+1/R_L}
}
\]

and, for \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v \simeq
+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})
\left(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L\right)
}
\]

The gain is positive: an increase in \(V_{\text{in}}\) raises the source voltage of \(M_2\), reduces \(V_{GS2}\), reduces the nMOS current, and causes \(V_{\text{out}}\) to rise.

---

## Input and output resistance

The familiar first-order common-gate input resistance is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}
}
\]

so the circuit has a relatively low input resistance.

Keeping finite \(r_o\), let

\[
R_X=r_{o1}\parallel R_L.
\]

Then the more exact result is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{R_X+r_{o2}}
{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}
}
\]

The intrinsic output resistance, with the input voltage source set to zero, is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}\simeq r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
}
\]

or \(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L\) if the load is included.

Thus, the circuit is a noninverting common-gate voltage amplifier with low input resistance, high output resistance, and gain approximately

\[
(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}).
\]

Its gain expression is equivalent to the required approximation; the extra detail does not contradict the topology or gain mechanism.

\;\Rightarrow\;
V_{GS2}\downarrow

Let the intermediate node between the transistors be \(v_x\), and define

\[
u \equiv V_{\text{in}}-V_T,
\qquad
\beta_i=\mu_n C_{\text{ox}}(W/L)_i .
\]

The drain current is

\[
I_D=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}.
\]

## 1. Operating regions

The transistor voltages are

\[
V_{GS1}=V_{\text{in}}, \quad V_{DS1}=v_x
\]

\[
V_{GS2}=V_{\text{in}}-v_x,\quad V_{DS2}=V_{\text{out}}-v_x.
\]

For \(M_2\) to conduct,

\[
V_{GS2}>V_T \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_x<u.
\]

But \(M_1\) would be saturated only if

\[
v_x\ge u.
\]

Thus, whenever the stack carries current, \(M_1\) cannot be in saturation; it operates in triode. The upper device behaves as follows:

- If \(V_{\text{out}}\ge u\), \(M_2\) is in saturation.
- If \(V_{\text{out}}<u\), \(M_2\) is in triode.

So this is not a conventional two-transistor cascode with both devices saturated.

---

## 2. Equivalent pull-down transistor

Under the ideal square-law model, the two tied-gate MOSFETs behave externally like one nMOS with

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\frac{1}{\beta_{\rm eq}}=\frac{1}{\beta_1}+\frac{1}{\beta_2}.
\]

For identical devices, \(\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta\),

\[
\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta}{2}.
\]

Thus the stack has half the effective strength of either individual transistor.

### Upper transistor saturated: \(V_{\text{out}}\ge u\)

The internal node is

\[
v_x=u\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\boxed{I_D=\frac{\beta_{\rm eq}}{2}u^2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{DD}
-\frac{R_D\beta_{\rm eq}}{2}
(V_{\text{in}}-V_T)^2
}
\]

provided that

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_{\text{in}}-V_T.
\]

For matched devices,

\[
v_x=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\right)(V_{\text{in}}-V_T),
\]

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{4}(V_{\text{in}}-V_T)^2.
\]

### Both transistors in triode: \(V_{\text{out}}<u\)

The current is

\[
\boxed{
I_D=\beta_{\rm eq}
\left[
uV_{\text{out}}-\frac{V_{\text{out}}^2}{2}
\right]
}
\]

and the load-line equation is

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}
=
\beta_{\rm eq}
\left[
uV_{\text{out}}-\frac{V_{\text{out}}^2}{2}
\right].
\]

The physical root is

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
\frac{
1+R_D\beta_{\rm eq}u
-
\sqrt{(1+R_D\beta_{\rm eq}u)^2
-2R_D\beta_{\rm eq}V_{DD}}
}{
R_D\beta_{\rm eq}
}
}
\]

for the region \(V_{\text{out}}<u\).

---

## 3. Logic behavior

This is a resistor-loaded nMOS inverter:

- \(V_{\text{in}}\le V_T\): both devices are off and
  \[
  V_{\text{out}}\approx V_{DD}.
  \]

- Increasing \(V_{\text{in}}\) turns on the stack, increasing pull-down current and reducing \(V_{\text{out}}\).

- At high input voltage, there is static current from \(V_{DD}\) through \(R_D\), \(M_2\), and \(M_1\) to ground.

The turn-on is near one threshold voltage, not \(2V_T\), because the intermediate node remains close to ground near turn-on.

---

## 4. Small-signal voltage gain

If the circuit is biased with \(M_2\) in saturation, and channel-length modulation is neglected,

\[
g_{m,\rm eq}
=
\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{\text{in}}}
=
\beta_{\rm eq}(V_{\text{in}}-V_T).
\]

Since \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground,

\[
\boxed{
A_v
=
\frac{dv_{\text{out}}}{dv_{\text{in}}}
\simeq
-g_{m,\rm eq}R_D
=
-R_D\beta_{\rm eq}(V_{\text{in}}-V_T)
}
\]

as long as \(M_2\) remains saturated.

If both devices are in triode,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{dv_{\text{out}}}{dv_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{R_D\beta_{\rm eq}V_{\text{out}}}
{1+R_D\beta_{\rm eq}(u-V_{\text{out}})}
}
\]

so the gain decreases as the output approaches ground.

---

## 5. Practical nonidealities

The compact \(\beta_{\rm eq}\) result assumes equal constant thresholds. In a normal CMOS process, the bulk of \(M_2\) is often tied to ground while its source is at \(v_x\). Thus \(M_2\) experiences body effect:

\[
V_{T2}=V_{T0}+
\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_F+v_x}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right).
\]

This raises its threshold and reduces the pull-down current. Channel-length modulation also gives the stack a finite output resistance.

So, physically, this is a tied-gate/self-cascode-like pull-down stack, but its ideal DC behavior is that of a weaker single nMOS transistor with effective parameter \(\beta_{\rm eq}\).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the tied-gate stack, with M1 in triode and M2 saturated in the relevant region, and derives the equivalent strength βeq = β1β2/(β1+β2). This is the longer-effective-channel relation (for equal widths, twice the channel length); it also correctly avoids treating the circuit as a conventional cascode.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are enhancement NMOS devices, with their gates tied to \(V_{\text{in}}\). Let

\[
v_x \equiv v_{D1}=v_{S2}
\]

be the intermediate node. Then

\[
V_{GS1}=v_i,\qquad V_{DS1}=v_x
\]

\[
V_{GS2}=v_i-v_x,\qquad V_{DS2}=v_o-v_x .
\]

This is a resistor-loaded NMOS inverter with a gate-tied series pair, often called a self-cascode pair.

## Operating regions

Let

\[
U=v_i-V_T .
\]

- If \(v_i\leq V_T\), both devices are off, so

\[
v_o=V_{DD}.
\]

- If \(v_i>V_T\), current flows from \(V_{DD}\) through \(R_D\), \(M_2\), and \(M_1\) to ground.

For matched devices and ignoring body effect:

- \(M_2\) can conduct only if \(v_x<U\).
- \(M_1\) would be saturated only if \(v_x\geq U\).

Thus, whenever the stack conducts, \(M_1\) is in the triode region. It is incorrect to assume that both transistors are saturated.

\(M_2\) is saturated if

\[
V_{DS2}\geq V_{GS2}-V_T
\]

or

\[
v_o-v_x\geq v_i-v_x-V_T,
\]

which reduces to

\[
\boxed{v_o\geq U.}
\]

If \(v_o<U\), both devices are in triode.

---

## Equivalent NMOS device

Define

\[
\beta_i=\mu_n C_{\text{ox}}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_i,
\]

using the convention

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}V_{OV}^2
\]

in saturation.

Ignoring channel-length modulation and body effect, the two gate-tied series devices behave like one NMOS with

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\text{eq}}=
\left(\frac{1}{\beta_1}+\frac{1}{\beta_2}\right)^{-1}
=\frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}.}
\]

For identical devices,

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\text{eq}}=\frac{\beta}{2}.}
\]

Thus, two identical series devices with tied gates act approximately like a single device of twice the channel length.

The stack current is therefore

\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\beta_{\text{eq}}}{2}U^2,
& v_o\geq U \quad (M_2\text{ saturated}),\\[1.1em]
\beta_{\text{eq}}\left(Uv_o-\dfrac{v_o^2}{2}\right),
& 0\leq v_o<U \quad (M_1,M_2\text{ triode}).
\end{cases}
\]

For equal devices in the saturated-output region,

\[
v_x=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\right)U,
\]

so \(M_1\) is indeed in triode and \(M_2\) is in saturation.

---

## DC transfer characteristic

The resistor load imposes

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_D}=I_D.
\]

Let

\[
q=R_D\beta_{\text{eq}}.
\]

Then the ideal voltage-transfer characteristic is

\[
v_o=
\begin{cases}
V_{DD}, & v_i\leq V_T,\\[0.8em]
V_{DD}-\dfrac{q}{2}(v_i-V_T)^2,
& v_o\geq v_i-V_T,\\[1.1em]
\dfrac{1+qU-\sqrt{(1+qU)^2-2qV_{DD}}}{q},
& v_o<U.
\end{cases}
\]

The transition between the last two regions occurs at \(v_o=U\), where

\[
U_B=
\frac{\sqrt{1+2qV_{DD}}-1}{q}.
\]

Hence the corresponding input voltage is

\[
V_{i,B}=V_T+U_B.
\]

Qualitatively,

\[
V_{\text{in}}\text{ low}\Rightarrow V_{\text{out}}\approx V_{DD},
\]

\[
V_{\text{in}}\text{ high}\Rightarrow V_{\text{out}}\text{ is pulled toward ground}.
\]

So the circuit implements an inverting transfer characteristic, but unlike CMOS logic it consumes static power when the input is high:

\[
P_{DD}=V_{DD}I_D.
\]

---

## Small-signal gain

If biased with \(M_2\) in saturation, the effective transconductance is

\[
g_{m,\text{eq}}=\beta_{\text{eq}}(V_{I,Q}-V_T).
\]

Ignoring channel-length modulation,

\[
\boxed{A_v\simeq -g_{m,\text{eq}}R_D.}
\]

For two identical devices,

\[
A_v\simeq -\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{I,Q}-V_T)R_D.
\]

With finite output resistance, \(R_D\) is replaced approximately by \(R_D\parallel r_{\text{stack}}\). The stack can provide some cascode-like output-resistance enhancement, but it is not a conventional cascode because the upper gate is driven by the input rather than held at a fixed bias.

If \(M_2\)'s body is tied to ground, its threshold increases as \(v_x\) rises because of body effect. Then the simple \(\beta_{\text{eq}}\) result is approximate, and the exact DC solution follows from

\[
I_{D1}(v_i,v_x)=I_{D2}(v_i-v_x,v_o-v_x)
=\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_D}.
\]

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS pair, places M1 in triode, and concludes that identical devices approximate a single NMOS with twice the channel length. The additional ideal-model analysis is consistent with that mechanism.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are enhancement nMOS transistors, this is a resistor-loaded nMOS inverter with two series pull-down devices whose gates are both driven by \(V_{\text{in}}\).

Let the node between the two transistors be \(V_X\).

\[
V_{GS1}=V_{\text{in}},\qquad V_{DS1}=V_X
\]

\[
V_{GS2}=V_{\text{in}}-V_X,\qquad V_{DS2}=V_{\text{out}}-V_X
\]

The dc current must satisfy

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}
=I_{D1}=I_{D2}.
\]

Thus, a numerical answer requires \(R_D\), \(V_{DD}\), transistor sizes, threshold voltages, etc. However, its operation can be described generally.

---

## Qualitative operation

- **\(V_{\text{in}}<V_T\):**  
  Both nMOS devices are off. No current flows in \(R_D\), so

  \[
  V_{\text{out}}\simeq V_{DD}.
  \]

  The intermediate node \(V_X\) is ideally floating.

- **\(V_{\text{in}}>V_T\):**  
  \(M_1\) turns on and pulls \(V_X\) down. This gives \(M_2\) a positive \(V_{GS2}\), so it also turns on. Current flows through

  \[
  V_{DD}\rightarrow R_D\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow M_1\rightarrow \text{ground},
  \]

  and \(V_{\text{out}}\) falls.

Thus, logically,

\[
V_{\text{out}}\approx \overline{V_{\text{in}}},
\]

provided the transistor stack is strong enough relative to \(R_D\).

---

## Ideal long-channel analysis

Neglect body effect and channel-length modulation, and define

\[
A=V_{\text{in}}-V_T,
\]

with the usual convention

\[
I_{D,\text{sat}}=\frac{\beta}{2}V_{OV}^{2}.
\]

For two devices with parameters \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\), the series stack behaves ideally like one nMOS transistor having

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\text{eq}}
=\frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}
\]

For identical devices,

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\text{eq}}=\frac{\beta}{2}}.
\]

So two matched series nMOS devices, with their gates tied together, have approximately half the strength of one device.

The stack current is then

\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
0, & A\leq 0\\[6pt]
\beta_{\text{eq}}
\left(A V_{\text{out}}-\dfrac{V_{\text{out}}^2}{2}\right),
& 0<V_{\text{out}}<A\\[10pt]
\dfrac{\beta_{\text{eq}}}{2}A^2,
& V_{\text{out}}\geq A
\end{cases}
\]

and the output voltage follows from the load line

\[
\boxed{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}=I_D.}
\]

In the high-output region, where the upper transistor is saturated,

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{DD}
-\frac{R_D\beta_{\text{eq}}}{2}
(V_{\text{in}}-V_T)^2
}
\]

valid while

\[
V_{\text{out}}\geq V_{\text{in}}-V_T.
\]

When the output becomes low, both transistors are in the triode region and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}
=
\beta_{\text{eq}}
\left[
(V_{\text{in}}-V_T)V_{\text{out}}
-\frac{V_{\text{out}}^2}{2}
\right].
\]

---

## Device regions

Under the ideal matched-device assumption:

- For finite current, \(M_1\) is normally in the **triode region**.
- If

  \[
  V_{\text{out}}\geq V_{\text{in}}-V_T,
  \]

  \(M_2\) is in saturation.

- If

  \[
  V_{\text{out}}<V_{\text{in}}-V_T,
  \]

  both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are in triode.

This is not a conventional cascode, since the gate of \(M_2\) is not held at a fixed bias; it is driven by the same input as \(M_1\).

---

## Practical remarks

- For a logic-high input, there is static current through \(R_D\), so this is not a low-static-power CMOS inverter.
- If \(M_2\)'s body is tied to ground, its source rises above ground and it experiences body effect:

  \[
  V_{T2}>V_{T1}.
  \]

  Therefore, the real pull-down strength is usually somewhat less than the ideal \(\beta/2\) result for matched devices.
- Around a bias point in the saturation-like region, the approximate small-signal gain is

  \[
  A_v \simeq -g_{m,\text{eq}}R_D,
  \qquad
  g_{m,\text{eq}}=\beta_{\text{eq}}(V_{\text{in}}-V_T).
  \]

So the circuit behaves as a weaker resistor-loaded common-source inverter/amplifier, with an effective nMOS strength roughly half that of either matched transistor alone.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS stack and its triode-lower/saturated-upper operation. The harmonic beta_{mathrm{eq}} relation, giving half strength for matched devices, is equivalent to the longer-effective-channel result; the additional inverter analysis is consistent with its stated ideal assumptions.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS source-coupled differential pair with a single-ended resistive output. \(M_1\) compares \(V_{in}\) against the reference/bias voltage \(V_b\); \(M_2\)'s drain current is converted to \(V_{out}\) by \(R_D\).

Let the tail current be

\[
I_T \equiv I_1 .
\]

Assume initially that \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are matched, both are in saturation, channel-length modulation is neglected, and the tail source is ideal.

## DC behavior

The tail current divides between the two transistors:

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_T
\]

and the output voltage is

\[
V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_D I_{D2}.
\]

Thus:

- If \(V_{in}>V_b\), \(M_1\) takes more current.
  - \(I_{D2}\) decreases.
  - The drop across \(R_D\) decreases.
  - \(V_{out}\) rises toward \(V_{DD}\).

- If \(V_{in}<V_b\), \(M_2\) takes more current.
  - \(I_{D2}\) increases.
  - The drop across \(R_D\) increases.
  - \(V_{out}\) falls.

So the circuit is noninverting with respect to \(V_{in}\):

\[
V_{in}\uparrow \quad \Longrightarrow \quad V_{out}\uparrow.
\]

For matched devices at \(V_{in}=V_b\),

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_T}{2}
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_T R_D}{2}}.
\]

The common-source node voltage at this bias point is

\[
V_S=V_b-V_T-\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta}},
\]

where the long-channel MOS model is taken as

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2.
\]

---

## Large-signal transfer characteristic

Define the differential input voltage

\[
v_d=V_{in}-V_b.
\]

For matched transistors, while both devices conduct,

\[
I_{D1}-I_{D2}
=
\sqrt{\beta I_T}\,v_d
\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta v_d^2}{4I_T}}.
\]

Since

\[
I_{D2}=\frac{I_T-(I_{D1}-I_{D2})}{2},
\]

the output is

\[
\boxed{
V_{out}
=
V_{DD}
-\frac{R_D}{2}
\left[
I_T-
\sqrt{\beta I_T}\,v_d
\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta v_d^2}{4I_T}}
\right]
}
\]

for

\[
|v_d| \leq \sqrt{\frac{2I_T}{\beta}}.
\]

At the current-steering limits:

\[
V_{in}-V_b \geq \sqrt{\frac{2I_T}{\beta}}
\]

gives approximately

\[
I_{D1}\simeq I_T,\qquad I_{D2}\simeq 0,
\qquad V_{out}\simeq V_{DD}.
\]

Conversely,

\[
V_{in}-V_b \leq -\sqrt{\frac{2I_T}{\beta}}
\]

gives approximately

\[
I_{D1}\simeq 0,\qquad I_{D2}\simeq I_T,
\qquad V_{out}\simeq V_{DD}-I_T R_D.
\]

Hence, it can also operate as a differential comparator whose nominal switching point is \(V_{in}=V_b\).

---

## Small-signal gain

At the balanced bias point,

\[
g_m=\sqrt{\beta I_T}
\]

is the transconductance of either transistor, since each carries \(I_T/2\).

For an ideal tail current source, small-signal KCL at the common-source node gives

\[
\tilde v_s=\frac{\tilde v_{in}+\tilde v_b}{2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\tilde i_{D2}
=
-\frac{g_m}{2}
(\tilde v_{in}-\tilde v_b).
\]

Because \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground,

\[
\tilde v_{out}=-R_D\tilde i_{D2}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
\tilde v_{out}
=
\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
(\tilde v_{in}-\tilde v_b)
}
\]

and, if \(V_b\) is AC-grounded,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{\tilde v_{out}}{\tilde v_{in}}
=
+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
}.
\]

More generally, if the two transistors have unequal transconductances,

\[
\frac{\tilde v_{out}}{\tilde v_{in}-\tilde v_b}
=
R_D\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}.
\]

Ignoring channel-length modulation,

\[
R_{in}\approx \infty,
\qquad
R_{out}\approx R_D.
\]

A finite transistor output resistance and output load reduce the gain; a common first-order replacement is \(R_D\rightarrow R_D\parallel r_{o2}\).

---

## Operating constraints

For \(M_2\) to remain in saturation,

\[
V_{out}\gtrsim V_b-V_T.
\]

For \(M_1\) to remain in saturation,

\[
V_{DD}\gtrsim V_{in}-V_T.
\]

Also, the current source must have enough voltage across it to remain an approximately constant current source. If these conditions are violated, the simple current-steering and gain expressions no longer apply.

In summary, this circuit is a resistor-loaded differential amplifier/current-steering comparator with nominal threshold \(V_b\), quiescent output \(V_{DD}-I_1R_D/2\), and small-signal gain approximately \(+g_mR_D/2\).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled differential pair, with M2 biased at Vb and its drain providing the resistive output. The current-steering behavior and non-inverting small-signal gain are also correct.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Let \(I_T \equiv I_1\). The circuit is an NMOS source-coupled (differential) pair with a resistive single-ended load at the drain of \(M_2\).

- \(M_1\) compares \(V_{\rm in}\)
- \(M_2\) compares the reference/bias \(V_b\)
- \(R_D\) converts the \(M_2\) drain current to \(V_{\rm out}\)

Thus, increasing \(V_{\rm in}\) steers tail current from \(M_2\) into \(M_1\), causing \(V_{\rm out}\) to rise. The circuit is therefore non-inverting with respect to \(V_{\rm in}\).

Assume matched MOSFETs, an ideal tail current source, both devices in saturation, negligible channel-length modulation, and

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2 .
\]

Define the differential input as

\[
v_d=V_{\rm in}-V_b.
\]

For both transistors on,

\[
V_S=\frac{V_{\rm in}+V_b}{2}-V_{TN}
-\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\frac{v_d^2}{4}},
\]

and the branch currents are

\[
I_{D1}=
\frac{I_T}{2}
+\frac{\beta_n v_d}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\frac{v_d^2}{4}},
\]

\[
I_{D2}=
\frac{I_T}{2}
-\frac{\beta_n v_d}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\frac{v_d^2}{4}}.
\]

The output is

\[
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-R_D I_{D2}.
\]

The two-transistor region is valid for

\[
|v_d|\leq V_X,
\qquad
V_X=\sqrt{\frac{2I_T}{\beta_n}}.
\]

Hence the large-signal transfer characteristic is

\[
V_{\rm out}=
\begin{cases}
V_{DD}-I_T R_D,
& V_{\rm in}-V_b\leq -V_X,\\[6pt]
V_{DD}-R_D\left[
\dfrac{I_T}{2}
-\dfrac{\beta_n v_d}{2}
\sqrt{\dfrac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\dfrac{v_d^2}{4}}
\right],
& |v_d|<V_X,\\[10pt]
V_{DD},
& V_{\rm in}-V_b\geq V_X.
\end{cases}
\]

So qualitatively:

| Condition | Current steering | Output |
|---|---|---|
| \(V_{\rm in}\ll V_b\) | \(M_2\) carries nearly all \(I_T\) | \(V_{\rm out}\approx V_{DD}-I_T R_D\) |
| \(V_{\rm in}=V_b\) | \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_T/2\) | \(V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-I_T R_D/2\) |
| \(V_{\rm in}\gg V_b\) | \(M_1\) carries nearly all \(I_T\) | \(V_{\rm out}\approx V_{DD}\) |

At the balanced bias point, \(V_{\rm in}=V_b\),

\[
V_{OV}=\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}},
\qquad
g_m=\sqrt{\beta_n I_T}.
\]

The small-signal gain is then

\[
\frac{\partial v_{\rm out}}{\partial (v_{\rm in}-v_b)}
=
R_D\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}},
\]

and for matched devices,

\[
A_v=\frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_{\rm in}}
\simeq +\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
\]

when \(V_b\) is AC-grounded. Thus near the switching point,

\[
V_{\rm out}\simeq
V_{DD}-\frac{I_T R_D}{2}
+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}(V_{\rm in}-V_b).
\]

Important headroom conditions are:

\[
V_{\rm out}\gtrsim V_b-V_{TN}
\]

for \(M_2\) to remain saturated, and the tail current source must have sufficient voltage across it. If

\[
V_{DD}-I_T R_D < V_b-V_{TN},
\]

\(M_2\) enters triode operation at low output voltage, and the square-law transfer expression no longer applies. Finite output resistance, mismatch, and a nonideal tail source also shift the midpoint and reduce the ideal gain.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled differential pair, with M2 biased by Vb and output taken at its drain. The current steering, non-inverting response, and small-signal gain are also correct.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is an NMOS source-coupled differential pair (current-steering pair) with a resistive single-ended output. The tail source fixes the total current, while \(R_D\) converts the current in \(M_2\) into \(V_{\text{out}}\).

Let

\[
I_T \equiv I_1,\qquad \Delta v=V_{\text{in}}-V_b
\]

and assume matched long-channel NMOS devices in saturation, negligible channel-length modulation, and

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2 .
\]

The fundamental relations are

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_T
\]

and

\[
V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}-R_D I_{D2}.
\]

Thus, current steered into \(M_2\) pulls the output down; current steered into \(M_1\) leaves \(R_D\) with little or no current, so the output rises toward \(V_{DD}\).

## Large-signal behavior

For both transistors on,

\[
I_{D2}
=
\frac{I_T}{2}
-\frac{\beta_n\Delta v}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\frac{\Delta v^2}{4}},
\]

valid for

\[
|\Delta v|\leq \sqrt{\frac{2I_T}{\beta_n}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{DD}
-
R_D\left[
\frac{I_T}{2}
-\frac{\beta_n\Delta v}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}-\frac{\Delta v^2}{4}}
\right].
\]

The limiting cases are more informative:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Input condition} & \text{Current steering} & V_{\text{out}} \\ \hline
V_{\text{in}} \ll V_b & M_2\text{ carries }I_T,\; M_1\text{ off}
& V_{DD}-I_T R_D \\[4pt]
V_{\text{in}}=V_b & I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_T/2
& V_{DD}-\dfrac{I_T R_D}{2} \\[8pt]
V_{\text{in}} \gg V_b & M_1\text{ carries }I_T,\; M_2\text{ off}
& \approx V_{DD}
\end{array}
\]

Hence the circuit behaves as a noninverting comparator/amplifier:

- \(V_{\text{in}}>V_b \Rightarrow V_{\text{out}}\) rises.
- \(V_{\text{in}}<V_b \Rightarrow V_{\text{out}}\) falls.

For matched devices, the switching point is \(V_{\text{in}}=V_b\).

## Small-signal gain about \(V_{\text{in}}=V_b\)

At the balanced bias point,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_T}{2},
\]

and the overdrive of either device is

\[
V_{OV}=\sqrt{\frac{I_T}{\beta_n}}.
\]

Thus,

\[
g_m=\beta_n V_{OV}=\sqrt{\beta_n I_T}.
\]

With an ideal tail current source, the common-source node moves by approximately

\[
\tilde v_s=\frac{\tilde v_{\text{in}}+\tilde v_b}{2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\tilde i_{d2}
=
-\frac{g_m}{2}
(\tilde v_{\text{in}}-\tilde v_b),
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\tilde v_{\text{out}}
=
\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
(\tilde v_{\text{in}}-\tilde v_b)
}
\]

Ignoring \(r_o\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{\partial v_{\text{out}}}{\partial v_{\text{in}}}
\simeq +\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
}
\]

when \(V_b\) is AC-grounded. The positive sign confirms that the stage is noninverting with respect to \(V_{\text{in}}\).

## Headroom conditions

For \(M_2\) to remain saturated,

\[
V_{\text{out}} \geq V_b-V_{TN}.
\]

At the balanced operating point, this requires

\[
V_{DD}-\frac{I_T R_D}{2}\geq V_b-V_{TN}.
\]

To keep \(M_2\) saturated even when it carries all of the tail current,

\[
V_{DD}-I_T R_D\geq V_b-V_{TN}.
\]

Also, the tail current source must have sufficient compliance voltage. If these conditions are violated, \(M_2\) or the tail source enters triode region and the square-law transfer and gain above no longer apply.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair with M2’s gate at Vb and output at M2’s drain. Its current-steering description and positive small-signal gain are also consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
\(M_1\) is used as a source follower: its drain is at \(V_{DD}\) (AC ground) and its source is \(V_{\text{out}}\). The important feedback path is therefore

\[
V_{\text{out}} \rightarrow C_{gs1} \rightarrow \text{gate of }M_1
\rightarrow R_S \rightarrow \text{AC ground}.
\]

To find \(Z_{\text{out}}\), set \(V_{\text{in}}=0\), so the left side of \(R_S\) is at AC ground. Ignore \(r_o\) and secondary capacitances for the moment, and apply a test voltage \(v_x\) at the output.

Let \(C=C_{gs1}\). The gate voltage is determined by

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC(v_g-v_x)=0,
\]

so

\[
v_g=\frac{sR_SC}{1+sR_SC}v_x.
\]

The current drawn from the test source at the source of \(M_1\) is

\[
i_x=(g_{m1}+sC)(v_x-v_g).
\]

Hence,

\[
Z_{\text{out}}=\frac{v_x}{i_x}
=\frac{1+sR_SC_{gs1}}{g_{m1}+sC_{gs1}}.
\]

The impedance has a zero and a pole:

\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{R_SC_{gs1}},
\qquad
\omega_p=\frac{g_{m1}}{C_{gs1}}.
\]

If

\[
g_{m1}R_S>1,
\]

then \(\omega_z<\omega_p\). Thus \(Z_{\text{out}}\) has phase lead, i.e., a positive imaginary part:

\[
\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{\text{out}}\}
=
\frac{\omega C_{gs1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}
{g_{m1}^2+(\omega C_{gs1})^2}>0.
\]

At sufficiently low frequency,

\[
Z_{\text{out}}
\approx
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
+s\frac{C_{gs1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}{g_{m1}^2}.
\]

This resembles a series resistance and inductance:

\[
R_{\text{out}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}},
\qquad
L_{\text{eq}}\approx
\frac{C_{gs1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}{g_{m1}^2}.
\]

So there is no physical inductor. Rather, \(C_{gs1}\), \(R_S\), and the transconductance of \(M_1\) create active feedback that can produce an effective negative output capacitance; when viewed as an impedance, that appears inductive.

Finite \(r_o\), \(C_{ds}\), the capacitances of \(M_2\), and load capacitance add ordinary shunt capacitance and may mask the effect, but the underlying inductive behavior occurs when the \(g_mR_S\) effect is sufficiently strong.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-follower topology and derives the expected output-impedance expression. It shows that the impedance is inductive when g_m1 R_S > 1 (equivalently, R_S > 1/g_m1), with positive imaginary part and the correct low-frequency equivalent inductance.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
\(M_1\) is a source follower. The important point is that, when finding \(Z_{\text{out}}\), \(V_{in}\) is set to zero, but the gate of \(M_1\) is not an ideal AC ground: it is connected to AC ground through the finite resistance \(R_S\).

Thus \(C_{gs1}\) feeds an output-voltage variation back to the gate.

Let \(v_x=v_{\text{out}}\), \(C=C_{gs1}\), and neglect other parasitics initially. With a test voltage applied at the output,

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC(v_g-v_x)=0
\]

so

\[
\frac{v_g}{v_x}=\frac{sR_SC}{1+sR_SC}.
\]

The current drawn from the output by the source follower is approximately

\[
i_x=(g_{m1}+sC)(v_x-v_g).
\]

Therefore,

\[
Y_{\text{out}}
=\frac{i_x}{v_x}
=\frac{g_{m1}+sC}{1+sR_SC},
\]

or

\[
Z_{\text{out}}
=\frac{1+sR_SC}{g_{m1}+sC}.
\]

At low frequency,

\[
Z_{\text{out}}
\approx
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
+s\,\frac{C(g_{m1}R_S-1)}{g_{m1}^2}.
\]

The second term has the form \(sL\). Hence, if

\[
g_{m1}R_S>1,
\]

the output impedance has a positive imaginary part and behaves inductively, with approximately

\[
L_{\text{eq}}
\approx
\frac{C_{gs1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}{g_{m1}^2}.
\]

Physically, an output-voltage change drives current through \(C_{gs1}\), producing a delayed/quadrature gate voltage across \(R_S\). The \(g_m\) action of \(M_1\) converts that gate-voltage component into a current that has the sign of a negative output capacitance. In parallel with the normal output conductance, that negative capacitive term gives a positive-reactance, or inductive, output impedance.

\(M_2\) mainly provides bias and contributes finite output resistance and parasitic capacitance. Those ordinary shunt capacitances can reduce or mask the inductive behavior, so the inductive region exists only over a finite frequency range.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower and derives the matching Zout expression. Its low-frequency expansion gives inductive behavior for gm1·RS > 1, with the correct equivalent inductance and physical mechanism; the exact expression also captures the high-frequency limit of RS.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
\(M_1\) is a source follower: its drain is at \(V_{DD}\) (AC ground) and its source is \(V_{\text{out}}\). The finite resistance \(R_S\) driving its gate is what allows an inductive-looking output impedance.

To find \(Z_{\text{out}}\), set \(V_{\text{in}}=0\), so the gate is connected to AC ground through \(R_S\). Ignore \(r_o\) and parasitics other than \(C_{GS1}\) for the moment, and apply a test voltage \(v_x\) at the output.

The gate voltage is determined by

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC_{GS1}(v_g-v_x)=0,
\]

so

\[
v_g=\frac{sR_SC_{GS1}}{1+sR_SC_{GS1}}v_x.
\]

The test current entering the output is

\[
i_x=(g_{m1}+sC_{GS1})(v_x-v_g).
\]

Therefore,

\[
Z_{\text{out}}
=\frac{v_x}{i_x}
=\frac{1+sR_SC_{GS1}}{g_{m1}+sC_{GS1}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
\frac{1+sR_SC_{GS1}}
{1+sC_{GS1}/g_{m1}}.
\]

For \(s=j\omega\),

\[
\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{\text{out}}\}
=
\frac{\omega C_{GS1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}
{g_{m1}^2+(\omega C_{GS1})^2}.
\]

Hence, if

\[
g_{m1}R_S>1,
\]

then \(\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{\text{out}}\}>0\), which is the signature of an inductive impedance.

At low frequency,

\[
Z_{\text{out}}
\approx
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
+s\underbrace{\frac{C_{GS1}}{g_{m1}^2}
(g_{m1}R_S-1)}_{L_{\text{eff}}}.
\]

Thus the source follower behaves approximately as a resistance \(1/g_{m1}\) in series with an effective inductance

\[
L_{\text{eff}}
=
\frac{C_{GS1}}{g_{m1}^2}(g_{m1}R_S-1).
\]

Physically, an output-voltage disturbance drives current through \(C_{GS1}\). That current develops a voltage across \(R_S\), moving the gate. The resulting \(g_m v_{gs}\) current provides a frequency-dependent feedback current that can overcompensate the ordinary capacitive current. The output current then lags the output voltage, just as it would for an inductor.

This is a synthetic, active inductance: the energy storage is still in transistor capacitances, while the transistor’s transconductance and DC bias create the inductive behavior. In a real circuit, \(C_{DB}\), \(C_{GD}\), load capacitance, and finite output resistances limit the frequency range over which the impedance appears inductive.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source follower and derives the right output-impedance expression. It gives the correct inductive condition, Rs > 1/gm, and explains the role of Cgs and the finite gate resistance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are nMOS devices with their sources and bodies at ground, the important connections are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& V_{GS} & V_{DS}\\ \hline
M_1 & V_X & V_{\text{out}}\\
M_2 & V_{\text{out}} & V_X
\end{array}
\]

Thus \(M_2\) is not simply in parallel with \(M_1\): its gate is driven by \(V_{\text{out}}\), while its drain is node \(X\). This creates positive feedback.

Let \(R_D=R_{D1}\), \(v_x=V_X\), and \(v_o=V_{\text{out}}\). Neglecting gate currents and any external output load, the DC equations are

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}(V_{GS2}=v_o,V_{DS2}=v_x)
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_D}
=
I_{D1}(V_{GS1}=v_x,V_{DS1}=v_o).
\]

These two nonlinear equations determine the possible DC operating points.

## Qualitative operation

For a small positive \(I_{\text{in}}\):

- \(M_2\) is on because its gate is near \(V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\) sinks the input current, keeping \(V_X\) low.
- \(M_1\) is off or weakly on.
- Therefore \(V_{\text{out}}\approx V_{DD}\).

As \(I_{\text{in}}\) increases:

1. \(V_X\) rises.
2. \(M_1\) turns on harder.
3. \(V_{\text{out}}\) falls.
4. The lower \(V_{\text{out}}\) weakens \(M_2\).
5. A weaker \(M_2\) allows \(V_X\) to rise even more.

Hence the feedback is regenerative:

\[
V_X\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{\text{out}}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_X\uparrow .
\]

The circuit is therefore a regenerative threshold element / negative-resistance cell, rather than an ordinary linear current-to-voltage converter.

---

## Small-signal analysis

At a DC bias point, define

\[
G_D=\frac{1}{R_D}+g_{ds1}.
\]

The small-signal node equations are

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{ds2}v_x+g_{m2}v_o
\]

and

\[
G_Dv_o+g_{m1}v_x=0.
\]

Solving,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{G_D}
{G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}}
{G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}}
}
\]

The critical quantity is

\[
\Delta=G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}.
\]

- If \(\Delta>0\), the operating point is locally nonregenerative.
- If \(\Delta=0\), the small-signal gain becomes very large; this is the switching or fold point.
- If \(\Delta<0\), the input node has negative incremental resistance and the circuit is regenerative/unstable in the linear sense.

The input resistance seen at \(X\) is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in},X}
=
\frac{1}{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}/G_D}
}
\]

so it becomes negative when

\[
\boxed{
g_{m1}g_{m2}>G_Dg_{ds2}.
}
\]

If \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\), then approximately

\[
R_{\text{in},X}\simeq
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}.
\]

This is the usual negative-resistance result for this topology.

---

## Example: high-output branch

Using the long-channel square-law model,

\[
I_D=\beta\left[(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]
\]

in triode and

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2
\]

in saturation.

Initially \(M_1\) is off, so \(v_o\simeq V_{DD}\). Normally \(M_2\) is then in triode, giving

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
\beta_2
\left[
(V_{DD}-V_{T2})v_x-\frac{v_x^2}{2}
\right].
\]

\(M_1\) begins to conduct when \(v_x=V_{T1}\), corresponding approximately to

\[
I_{\text{in,on}}
=
\beta_2
\left[
(V_{DD}-V_{T2})V_{T1}
-\frac{V_{T1}^2}{2}
\right].
\]

That is only the onset of \(M_1\) conduction; the actual regenerative transition generally occurs later, when

\[
G_Dg_{ds2}=g_{m1}g_{m2}.
\]

For the common region in which \(M_1\) is saturated and \(M_2\) is triode,

\[
v_o=V_{DD}
-\frac{R_D\beta_1}{2}(v_x-V_{T1})^2
\]

and the switching point satisfies

\[
V_{DD}-V_{T2}-v_x
=
\frac{R_D\beta_1}{2}
(v_x-V_{T1})(3v_x-V_{T1}).
\]

Substituting that \(v_x\) into the current expression gives the rising-current trip value.

---

## Important practical point

A DC state with \(M_2\) completely off cannot support a nonzero ideal \(I_{\text{in}}\), because node \(X\) then has no DC path:

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}
\]

would not be satisfiable.

Consequently, after regeneration drives \(M_2\) off, the eventual low-output state is determined by nonshown effects:

- current-source compliance,
- capacitance at node \(X\),
- leakage/subthreshold current,
- a reset or bleed path,
- finite output resistance of the input source.

So the shown circuit is a regenerative/negative-resistance cell, but a complete static Schmitt trigger or latch requires the input-source model and usually a reset/discharge path at \(X\).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are NMOS devices with their sources grounded, the important connections are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & V_{GS} & V_{DS}\\ \hline
M_1 & V_X & V_{\text{out}}\\
M_2 & V_{\text{out}} & V_X
\end{array}
\]

Thus, \(M_1\) is a resistively loaded common-source stage, and \(M_2\) feeds its output back to node \(X\). The circuit is a cross-coupled, positive-feedback structure.

## DC equations

Because MOS gates draw essentially zero DC current,

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}
\]

at node \(X\), and at the output node,

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}.
\]

Hence the general DC equations are

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
I_{D2}\left(V_{GS2}=V_{\text{out}},\,V_{DS2}=V_X\right)
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=
I_{D1}\left(V_{GS1}=V_X,\,V_{DS1}=V_{\text{out}}\right).
\]

These equations must be solved using the proper MOSFET region equations.

---

## Both transistors in saturation

With

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2,
\]

and neglecting channel-length modulation,

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2})^2,
\]

so that

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{T2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=
\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{T1})^2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
V_X
=
V_{T1}
+
\sqrt{
\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_{D1}}
}
}
\]

provided that the saturation conditions hold:

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{T1},
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2}.
\]

If either condition fails, the corresponding transistor must be analyzed in triode region.

---

## Small-signal analysis

Let

\[
G_1=\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}.
\]

For small signals, \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground. At the output,

\[
G_1v_{\text{out}}+g_{m1}v_x=0,
\]

thus

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_x}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}}{G_1}
}
\]

which is the gain of \(M_1\).

At node \(X\),

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{o2}v_x+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

Substitution gives

\[
i_{\text{in}}
=
\left(
g_{o2}
-
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{G_1}
\right)v_x.
\]

Therefore, the incremental resistance seen by the input current source is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{1}
{
g_{o2}
-\dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{1/R_{D1}+g_{o1}}
}
}
\]

and the current-to-output-voltage gain is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}}
{
g_{m1}g_{m2}
-
(1/R_{D1}+g_{o1})g_{o2}
}
}.
\]

If \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}\simeq-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\simeq\frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
}
\]

---

## Positive feedback and stability

A rise in \(V_X\):

1. increases the current of \(M_1\),
2. lowers \(V_{\text{out}}\),
3. decreases the current of \(M_2\),
4. leaves more of \(I_{\text{in}}\) available to charge node \(X\),
5. raises \(V_X\) further.

Thus the loop is regenerative, i.e. positive feedback.

The approximate loop-gain magnitude is

\[
\boxed{
T \simeq
g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2}.
}
\]

The circuit exhibits negative incremental resistance and tends toward regeneration when

\[
\boxed{
g_{m1}g_{m2}
>
\left(\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}\right)g_{o2}.
}
\]

With ideal saturated MOSFETs, \(g_{o2}\) is very small, so this condition is often easily met. In that case, the DC solution obtained from the saturation equations can be an unstable equilibrium; parasitic capacitances, transistor triode operation, current-source compliance, and device nonlinearities determine the final state.

So this circuit is best viewed as a cross-coupled positive-feedback/negative-resistance cell rather than an ordinary linear amplifier.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are nMOS devices as drawn:

- Their gates are tied together at node \(X\).
- Their drains are tied together at \(V_{\text{out}}\).
- Their sources are grounded.
- Thus, electrically, they are two parallel common-source nMOS transistors loaded by \(R_{D1}\).

Let \(v_x=V_X\) and \(v_o=V_{\text{out}}\). The output-node equation is

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}(v_x,v_o)+I_{D2}(v_x,v_o).
\]

So, for a specified gate voltage \(v_x\), increasing \(v_x\) increases the pull-down current and lowers \(v_o\).

For matched devices with

\[
\beta_\Sigma=\beta_1+\beta_2,
\]

and neglecting channel-length modulation, if both devices are in saturation,

\[
I_D=\frac{1}{2}\beta_\Sigma(v_x-V_T)^2,
\]

hence

\[
\boxed{
v_o=V_{DD}-\frac{R_{D1}\beta_\Sigma}{2}(v_x-V_T)^2
}
\]

valid while

\[
v_o\ge v_x-V_T.
\]

If the devices enter triode operation, then

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}
=
\beta_\Sigma\left[(v_x-V_T)v_o-\frac{v_o^2}{2}\right].
\]

For identical transistors, the pair is equivalent to one transistor having twice the effective \(W/L\).

---

## Crucial issue: no DC operating point for nonzero \(I_{\rm in}\)

At node \(X\),

\[
I_{\rm in}=I_{G1}+I_{G2}.
\]

For ideal MOSFETs,

\[
I_{G1}=I_{G2}=0.
\]

Therefore, at DC,

\[
\boxed{I_{\rm in}=0}
\]

is required for a static operating point. A nonzero DC current injected into \(X\) has no resistive DC path to ground. It charges the MOS gate capacitances instead.

Thus, as drawn:

- There is no well-defined DC relation \(V_{\text{out}}(I_{\rm in})\).
- For constant positive \(I_{\rm in}\), \(v_x\) rises with time until leakage, an ESD clamp, gate-oxide breakdown, or the current source compliance limit becomes relevant.
- The output starts near \(V_{DD}\) if the transistors are initially off, then falls as \(v_x\) rises above threshold.

With gate capacitances included, approximately,

\[
I_{\rm in}\simeq C_{\rm eff}\frac{dv_x}{dt},
\]

where, including Miller effect,

\[
C_{\rm eff}\approx
C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gb1}+C_{gb2}
+(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})(1-A_v).
\]

Hence,

\[
v_x(t)\approx v_x(0)+\frac{I_{\rm in}}{C_{\rm eff}}t,
\]

and \(v_o(t)\) follows the nonlinear common-source transfer characteristic above.

For a small-signal voltage applied at \(X\), the voltage gain is approximately

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{v_x}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
{1/R_{D1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
}
\]

or, if \(r_o\) is large,

\[
\frac{v_o}{v_x}\approx -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})R_{D1}.
\]

So the circuit is a parallel-nMOS common-source stage, but the current source at \(X\) does not establish a DC bias unless a leakage/bias path from \(X\) is added.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume midband small-signal operation, both MOSFETs in saturation, \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_b\) are ac grounds, and \(r_o\) is initially neglected.

Let \(v_s\) denote the input/source node of \(M_1\).

- \(M_1\) is a common-gate stage.
- \(M_2\) is a common-source stage.
- \(R_F\) returns output voltage as a current at the input node.

Thus this is a **shunt-shunt negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier**.

For a positive incremental \(I_{\rm in}\), \(v_x\) rises, \(M_2\) draws more current, and \(v_{\rm out}\) falls. The resulting feedback current through \(R_F\) opposes the input current.

---

## Usual feedback analysis

Let \(i_e\) be the signal current processed by \(M_1\). Neglecting loading by \(R_F\),

\[
i_e=I_{\rm in}+i_{RF}
\]

\[
v_x \simeq R_{D1} i_e
\]

\[
v_{\rm out}\simeq -g_{m2}R_{D2}v_x
\]

Hence the open-loop transimpedance is

\[
Z_{t0}\equiv \frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_e}
\simeq -g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}.
\]

Since the input node is approximately at ac ground,

\[
i_{RF}\simeq \frac{v_{\rm out}}{R_F}.
\]

Define the loop-gain magnitude as

\[
\boxed{
L=\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}
}
\]

Then

\[
i_e=\frac{I_{\rm in}}{1+L}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{I_{\rm in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
{1+\dfrac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}}
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{I_{\rm in}}
=
-R_F\frac{L}{1+L}.
}
\]

Therefore, if \(L\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{
v_{\rm out}\simeq -I_{\rm in}R_F.
}
\]

The result is a transimpedance set mainly by \(R_F\), rather than by transistor parameters.

For the feedback-current arrow shown in the figure,

\[
\boxed{
i_{RF}=-\frac{L}{1+L}I_{\rm in}.
}
\]

Thus, for large loop gain, \(i_{RF}\approx -I_{\rm in}\): almost all of the input current is diverted through \(R_F\), while only a small error current flows through \(M_1\).

Also,

\[
v_x\simeq \frac{R_{D1}I_{\rm in}}{1+L}.
\]

---

## Input and output resistances

Using the usual feedback approximation,

\[
R_{\rm in,0}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m1}}
\]

without feedback. With feedback,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m1}(1+L)}.
}
\]

Thus the circuit has a low input resistance, as expected for a current-input/transimpedance amplifier.

Similarly, if \(R_F\) does not significantly load the output,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}\simeq \frac{R_{D2}}{1+L}.
}
\]

Both input and output resistances are reduced, characteristic of shunt-shunt feedback.

---

## Exact small-signal result including \(R_F\) loading

If the loading of \(R_F\) cannot be ignored, define

\[
R_1=R_{D1},\qquad R_2=R_{D2},\qquad
g_1=g_{m1},\qquad g_2=g_{m2}.
\]

The nodal equations are

\[
v_x=g_1R_1v_s
\]

\[
i_{\rm in}=g_1v_s+\frac{v_s-v_{\rm out}}{R_F}
\]

\[
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{R_2}+g_2v_x+
\frac{v_{\rm out}-v_s}{R_F}=0.
\]

Let

\[
D=1+g_1(R_F+R_2)+g_1g_2R_1R_2.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}
=
\frac{R_2\left(1-g_1g_2R_1R_F\right)}
{1+g_1(R_F+R_2)+g_1g_2R_1R_2}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}
=
\frac{R_F+R_2}
{1+g_1(R_F+R_2)+g_1g_2R_1R_2}.
}
\]

For sufficiently large gain, these exact expressions also reduce to

\[
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}\approx -R_F.
\]

---

The result applies only while both transistors remain in saturation and the output does not clip. For NMOS devices, the approximate saturation conditions are

\[
V_X\ge V_b-V_{T1},
\qquad
V_{\rm out}\ge V_X-V_{T2}.
\]

Thus, the circuit is a negative-feedback TIA whose ideal closed-loop gain is \(-R_F\).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume both MOSFETs are biased in saturation, \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_b\) are ac grounds, and initially neglect \(r_o\), body effect, and capacitances.

Let \(v_s\) denote the source node of \(M_1\), \(v_x\) the node \(X\), and \(v_o=v_{\text{out}}\). Define

\[
g_1=g_{m1},\qquad g_2=g_{m2}.
\]

\(M_1\) is a common-gate stage and \(M_2\) is a common-source stage.

### Small-signal equations

At node \(X\),

\[
\frac{v_x}{R_{D1}}-g_1v_s=0
\]

so

\[
v_x=g_1R_{D1}v_s.
\]

At the output node,

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_{D2}}+\frac{v_o-v_s}{R_F}+g_2v_x=0.
\]

At the input/source node,

\[
i_{\text{in}}
=
g_1v_s+\frac{v_s-v_o}{R_F}.
\]

The first stage is noninverting from \(v_s\) to \(v_x\), while \(M_2\) inverts. Thus, an increase in \(v_s\) pulls \(v_o\) down. The resistor \(R_F\) then removes current from the input node, so the feedback is negative.

---

## Closed-loop transimpedance

Define the open-loop transresistance magnitude

\[
R_m \equiv g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}.
\]

With \(R_F\) open,

\[
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}=-R_m.
\]

Solving the three node equations with \(R_F\) included gives

\[
\boxed{
Z_T\equiv \frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{R_{D2}-g_{m1}R_mR_F}
{1+g_{m1}\left(R_m+R_{D2}+R_F\right)}
}
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{R_{D2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_F}
{1+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}R_F+
g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
}.
\]

Normally,

\[
g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F \gg 1,
\]

so the active inverted path dominates and \(v_o\) decreases for a positive upward \(i_{\text{in}}\).

---

## Input resistance

The small-signal input resistance at the source of \(M_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
Z_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{v_s}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{R_{D2}+R_F}
{1+g_{m1}\left(R_m+R_{D2}+R_F\right)}
}
\]

which can also be written as

\[
\boxed{
Z_{\text{in}}^{-1}
=
g_{m1}\left(1+T_0\right)
+\frac{1}{R_{D2}+R_F}
}
\]

where

\[
\boxed{
T_0=
\frac{R_m}{R_{D2}+R_F}
=
\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_{D2}+R_F}
}
\]

is the low-frequency loop-gain magnitude with the loading of \(R_F\) included.

Thus, feedback lowers the input resistance. If the passive term is negligible,

\[
Z_{\text{in}}\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m1}(1+T_0)}.
\]

---

## High-loop-gain result

If the source node is nearly a virtual ac ground, i.e. \(1/g_{m1}\) is small enough, then

\[
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
\simeq
-R_F\frac{T_0}{1+T_0}.
\]

Therefore, for strong feedback \((T_0\gg 1)\),

\[
\boxed{
v_o \simeq -i_{\text{in}}R_F
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
Z_{\text{in}}\ll \frac{1}{g_{m1}}.
}
\]

This is the usual transimpedance-amplifier result: the feedback resistor sets the closed-loop transimpedance.

If \(R_F\gg R_{D2}\), then

\[
T_0\simeq \frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F},
\]

and the familiar form is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
\simeq
-\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
{1+\dfrac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}}
}.
\]

---

## Output resistance

With the input current source deactivated (opened),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}
=
\left[
\frac{1}{R_{D2}}
+
\frac{g_{m1}\left(1+g_{m2}R_{D1}\right)}
{1+g_{m1}R_F}
\right]^{-1}
}
\]

under the same ideal-MOS assumptions. Hence shunt-shunt feedback reduces both input and output resistance.

---

## Feedback current

If \(i_{RF}\) is defined from the output toward the input node, as drawn,

\[
i_{RF}=\frac{v_o-v_s}{R_F},
\]

and

\[
\frac{i_{RF}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{1+g_{m1}R_m}
{1+g_{m1}(R_m+R_{D2}+R_F)}.
\]

For strong feedback,

\[
i_{RF}\simeq -i_{\text{in}},
\]

meaning nearly all of the input signal current is balanced by the feedback current through \(R_F\).

---

This is therefore a **shunt-shunt negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier**. At high frequency, transistor capacitances introduce poles at \(X\) and the output, so stability and phase margin must be checked separately.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume small-signal operation, with \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_b\) as ac grounds, neglecting body effect and initially neglecting \(r_o\). Let

\[
v_s=\text{voltage at the source of }M_1,\qquad v_x=\text{node }X,\qquad v_o=v_{\text{out}}.
\]

This is a **shunt–shunt feedback transimpedance amplifier**: an input current is converted to an output voltage, with \(R_F\) providing negative feedback.

## Small-signal node equations

For \(M_1\), since its gate is at ac ground,

\[
v_{gs1}=-v_s.
\]

KCL at node \(X\) gives

\[
\frac{v_x}{R_{D1}}-g_{m1}v_s=0,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{v_x=g_{m1}R_{D1}v_s.}
\]

Thus, an increase in \(v_s\) raises node \(X\).

At the output node,

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_{D2}}+g_{m2}v_x+\frac{v_o-v_s}{R_F}=0.
\]

Substituting \(v_x=g_{m1}R_{D1}v_s\),

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_{D2}}
+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}v_s
+\frac{v_o-v_s}{R_F}=0.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{v_s}
=
\frac{R_{D2}\left(1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F\right)}
{R_F+R_{D2}}
}
\]

The input-node KCL is

\[
i_{\text{in}}
=
g_{m1}v_s+\frac{v_s-v_o}{R_F}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{v_s}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\left[
g_{m1}
+
\frac{1+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
{R_F+R_{D2}}
\right]^{-1}
}
\]

and the exact low-frequency transimpedance is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{
R_{D2}\left(1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F\right)
}
{
1+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})
+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}
}
}
\]

under the stated approximations.

---

## High-loop-gain result

If the two-transistor gain is sufficiently large, i.e., roughly,

\[
g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\gg 1,
\]

and the feedback dominates the input-node behavior, then \(v_s\) is held near a virtual ac ground. Nearly all of the input current flows through \(R_F\):

\[
i_{RF}\simeq i_{\text{in}}.
\]

Since the feedback current flows from the input node toward the output for positive \(i_{\text{in}}\),

\[
\frac{v_s-v_o}{R_F}\simeq i_{\text{in}}.
\]

With \(v_s\simeq 0\),

\[
\boxed{v_{\text{out}}\simeq -i_{\text{in}}R_F.}
\]

Thus the circuit behaves as an inverting current-to-voltage converter with transimpedance

\[
\boxed{Z_T \equiv \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\simeq -R_F.}
\]

The negative sign follows from the signal path:

\[
i_{\text{in}}\uparrow
\Rightarrow v_x\uparrow
\Rightarrow i_{D2}\uparrow
\Rightarrow v_{\text{out}}\downarrow.
\]

So \(R_F\) sets the closed-loop transimpedance, while \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(R_{D1}\), and \(R_{D2}\) provide the gain needed to make the approximation accurate.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate input behavior, the X-driven second stage, and RF feedback from output to input, with negative-feedback transimpedance approaching −RF. The small-signal equations are consistent with the stated approximations.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Let \(v_x\) denote the lower internal node. The lower downward current source is unlabeled in the figure; denote its magnitude by \(I_B\).

A key connection is that \(V_{\text{out}}\) is connected to the **gate of \(M_2\)**.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 & \text{Drain} & \text{Gate} & \text{Source}\\ \hline
M_1\;(\text{nMOS}) & V_{\text{out}} & V_b & v_x\\
M_2\;(\text{pMOS}) & v_x & V_{\text{out}} & V_{DD}
\end{array}
\]

Assume ideal current sources, no dc load at \(V_{\text{out}}\), and both MOSFETs operate in saturation.

## DC current balance

Since the gate of \(M_2\) draws no dc current, KCL at the output gives

\[
I_{D1}=I_1 .
\]

At node \(v_x\),

\[
I_B=I_{\text{in}}+I_{D1}+I_{D2},
\]

so that

\[
\boxed{I_{D2}=I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}.}
\]

Here \(I_{D2}\) is the positive pMOS current flowing from \(V_{DD}\) into node \(v_x\).

Thus, \(M_1\) current is fixed by \(I_1\), while \(M_2\) absorbs the current difference produced by \(I_{\text{in}}\).

---

## Ideal square-law result

Using

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}V_{OV}^2,
\]

with \(\beta_n=\mu_n C_{\rm ox}(W/L)_1\) and
\(\beta_p=\mu_p C_{\rm ox}(W/L)_2\),

\[
I_1=\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_b-v_x-V_{TN})^2,
\]

and hence

\[
\boxed{
v_x
=
V_b-V_{TN}
-\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_n}}
}
\]

Thus, \(M_1\) holds the input node \(v_x\) approximately constant.

For \(M_2\),

\[
I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}-|V_{TP}|\right)^2 .
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|
-\sqrt{
\frac{2\left(I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}\right)}
{\beta_p}
}
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{in}}
=
I_B-I_1
-\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}-|V_{TP}|\right)^2
}
\]

A positive increase in \(I_{\text{in}}\), in the direction shown, reduces the required current of \(M_2\). Therefore \(V_{\text{out}}\) rises.

---

## Small-signal behavior

Around a bias point, with \(V_b\), \(V_{DD}\), \(I_1\), and \(I_B\) treated as ac-fixed, define

\[
g_{oi}=\frac{1}{r_{oi}}.
\]

The small-signal equations are

\[
g_{o1}\tilde v_o-(g_{m1}+g_{o1})\tilde v_x=0
\]

and

\[
g_{m2}\tilde v_o+g_{o2}\tilde v_x=\tilde i_{\text{in}}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\tilde v_o}{\tilde i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}+g_{o1}}
{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})+g_{o1}g_{o2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{\tilde v_x}{\tilde i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{o1}}
{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{o1})+g_{o1}g_{o2}}
}
\]

For \(g_m r_o\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{\frac{\tilde v_o}{\tilde i_{\text{in}}}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m2}}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}}
}
\]

Thus, the circuit behaves as a regulated low-input-impedance current input and a current-to-voltage converter with approximately \(1/g_{m2}\) transimpedance.

The ideal-model result is valid only while

\[
I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}>0,
\]

and both transistors remain in saturation:

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_b-V_{TN},
\]

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge v_x-|V_{TP}|,
\]

\[
V_{\text{out}}\le V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|.
\]

A numerical value of \(V_{\text{out}}\) requires the value of the unlabeled bias current \(I_B\), device parameters, and any load connected to \(V_{\text{out}}\).
